rationale: The printed texts strongly support the entry’s central identification of destructive floodwaters with peoples or armies in motion. Isaiah 8:7 explicitly identifies the overflowing waters with the king of Assyria and his power, while Jeremiah 47:2 depicts an attacking force from the north as an overflowing flood. On the ordinary reading of Daniel 9:26, the flood likewise characterizes the destructive advance of the coming prince’s people. Thus the common Noahic interpretation—judgment, remnant salvation, baptism, and new creation—does not explain these particular military uses better. However, the entry’s additional claim that the flood can be the Lord’s own host sweeping the enemy away is not adequately established by its printed references. That branch depends principally on the chapter’s disputed reinterpretation of Daniel 9:26, whereas the verse’s natural syntax makes “the people of the prince that shall come” the destroyers of the city and sanctuary.
book_core_identification: Destroying floodwaters signify peoples in motion, particularly an army or nation advancing destructively.
book_secondary_elaborations: The moving people may be an invading nation.
The moving people may be the Lord’s own host sweeping an enemy away.
unsupported_glossary_assertions: The printed references do not adequately support the alternative that the flood is the Lord’s own host sweeping the enemy away.
chapter_only_objections: The chapter’s claim that the singular destroying verb in Daniel 9:26 has the Messiah as its subject is grammatically strained; the natural subject is the singular collective “people of the prince that shall come.”

The chapter’s broader claims of a nearly uniform sea/waters symbolism and its numerous applications to miracles, ritual objects, and Revelation extend far beyond what the glossary entry asserts and are not adjudicated here.
strongest_counter_interpretation: In these passages, a flood is a conventional image for overwhelming military invasion or destruction, especially by an enemy army; it need not encode a universal rule that waters equal peoples, and Daniel 9:26 does not depict the Lord’s host destroying the invaders.
counter_core_identification: The flood denotes an overwhelming enemy invasion or its destructive force.
material_core_denial: The strongest counter-reading does not materially deny the entry’s minimum core identification; it chiefly rejects the secondary Lord’s-host branch and questions whether the people symbolism should be generalized beyond these contexts.
counter_case: Isaiah 8:7 directly names Assyria, so the image can be understood simply as the overwhelming advance of an enemy empire.
Jeremiah 47:2 naturally depicts a northern invasion as a flood, emphasizing irresistible force and extent.
Daniel 9:26 most naturally says that the coming prince’s people destroy the city and sanctuary, with “a flood” describing that devastation rather than a counterattack by Messiah’s host.
The Noahic flood and other biblical water imagery show that “flood” is not everywhere reducible to an army or moving people.
book_explanatory_advantages: It identifies the concrete referent explicitly supplied by Isaiah: the waters are Assyria’s king and power in motion.
It unifies Isaiah 8:7, Jeremiah 47:2, and the ordinary military reading of Daniel 9:26 more specifically than the abstract label “overwhelming destruction.”
It explains why invading peoples are portrayed as waters that rise, overflow boundaries, cover land, and sweep through cities.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It follows the natural grammar and conventional reading of Daniel 9:26 without transferring the destroying action to the Messiah.
It avoids turning a recurrent military metaphor into an exceptionless symbolic definition.
It accommodates Noahic, baptismal, eschatological, chaos-water, and personal-distress uses of flood imagery outside the printed references.
unresolved_objections: The precise force of “flood” in Daniel 9:26 remains debated, though its ordinary reading supports invading people more readily than the Lord’s host.
The evidence establishes the military sense in the cited passages but does not establish that every scriptural flood has this meaning.
